feedback: If a learner multiplied 36 × 4 = 144: ask them to shade 36 as the big bar split into 4 equal parts; one part is the unknown number, so it must be smaller than 36, forcing division.
If the drawing shows the referent as larger than the n-times total, prompt: 'Which quantity is made of several copies of the other? That is the bigger one.'
When correct, ask them to state in words why they divided: 'The total of 4 copies is known, so I split it into 4 to find one copy.'
activities.intendedInsight: The position of the unknown in the comparison — not the presence of the word 'times' — decides whether you multiply or divide. A bar model (or number line) makes that position visible.
learnerActions: Read a comparison story, e.g. '36 is 4 times a number — what is the number?'

Draw a referent bar (the quantity being compared to) and an 'n-times' bar made of that many equal copies; a double number line or a ×n/÷n scale-factor arrow represents the same scaling relationship if you prefer.
Place a '?' marker on whichever bar is unknown.

Decide the operation from the position of the '?': if the whole n-times bar is unknown, multiply; if the referent or the number of copies is unknown, divide. For '36 is 4 times a number', the referent is unknown, so 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
Write the matching equation with a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 36 = 4 × n, then n = 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
Check: does your scale factor really map the referent to the compared quantity? (4 × 9 = 36.)
activities.title: Build the bar, place the unknown, decide × or ÷

feedback: If both stories get the same answer (e.g. 8 for both), have the learner build both with cubes or bars side by side; the two towers come out visibly different (8 vs 15), exposing that the operations must differ.

If the reverse ribbon problem gives 36 (12 × 3), point out that red would then be LONGER than blue, yet blue being 3 times as long as red means red must be the shorter one; the bar of 3 equal parts forces division.
When correct, ask them to generate their own matched pair — producing one that genuinely differs confirms they parse the structure.
activities.intendedInsight: 'More than' means add a fixed amount; 'times as many' means repeat the quantity. The same numbers give different answers, so you must read the comparison structure, not just spot a keyword — and which quantity is unknown decides whether you multiply or divide.
learnerActions: Solve two near-identical stories built on the same numbers: (a) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 MORE than Maya — how many does Tom have?' and (b) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 TIMES as many as Maya — how many does Tom have?'
Build or draw both: for (a), Maya's bar plus 5 more; for (b), 5 copies of Maya's bar.
State in your own words why the two differ, then make up your own matched 'more'/'times' pair and solve both.
Try a reverse problem: 'A blue ribbon is 12 cm. That is 3 times as long as the red ribbon. How long is the red ribbon?' Build blue as 3 equal parts; one part is red, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm.

Then try the forward direction: 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 4 cm — how long is blue?' Here the whole n-times bar is unknown, so 3 × 4 = 12 cm. Notice the operation ran the opposite way from the reverse problem.
activities.title: Matched pair: 'more than' versus 'times as many'

feedback: If a learner selects 144 for '36 is 4 times a number', return them to a bar of 36 split into 4 equal parts to see one part is 9.
If they classify a 'times as many' story as additive, re-read aloud and ask whether Tom's amount is Maya's amount repeated or Maya's amount plus a fixed number.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding the comparison type and the unknown's position up front determines the operation; this is checkable and should be practised across varied contexts.
learnerActions: Given a mixed set of comparison stories, sort each into 'multiplicative' or 'additive' before solving.
Match each story to an equation written with a symbol for the unknown.
Solve for the unknown wherever it sits — compared quantity, referent, or scale factor.
Check targeted traps: for '36 is 4 times a number, the number is…', confirm the answer is smaller than 36 (9), not larger (144).
activities.title: Sort, match, and solve mixed problems

feedback: If a learner jumps to an operation, ask them first to say which bar would be unknown in a drawing.
Prompt 'so do we multiply or divide to find the missing one?' and have them tie the answer back to the referent.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the comparison type and which quantity is known is the parsing step that controls the operation.
learnerActions: With a partner or guide, work a comparison story aloud, answering: 'Is this times as many or more than? Which quantity do we already know — the single amount or the repeated total?'
Decide together whether to multiply or divide, and justify the choice before computing.
Pose fresh contexts (heights, collections, lengths) and parse each one aloud.
activities.title: Talk it through: which quantity do we know?
